newsitem.title: UK: British banks spurn rival's anti-land mine pact.
newsitem.headline: British banks spurn rival's anti-land mine pact.

text.p: A British bank that trades on its image as Britain's ethical bank called on its competitors to agree to stop financing land mines, but a majority of them refused, with some saying the call was a marketing gimmick.

The Cooperative Bank said Thursday it asked almost 100 banks to sign the agreement, but only a handful agreed. Among the more than 90 that refused, some threatened legal action if they were identified, effectively preventing The Cooperative from naming those who signed up, the bank said.
"The response from other banks is clearly disappointing, and they appear to have missed a geniune opportunity to join us and set an example to the world's financial community," the bank said.
Britain's major banks dismissed the appeal as a "gimmick."
"It's slightly strange for The Cooperative to expect all banks to endorse its marketing campaign," said a spokeswoman for Midland Bank, a unit of HSBC Holdings Plc.

Midland, National Westminster Bank and Barclays all said their lending policies were in line with a British government moratorium on exports of land mines. "We fully support the United Nations' efforts to end the use of land mines around the world," a Barclays spokeswoman said.
The Cooperative says government measures are inadequate. It asked the banks to pledge that they would not indirectly finance the manufacture, production, stockpiling or trade of land mines.
"National and international law is widely acknowledged to be woefully inadequate in this area," the Cooperative said.
The chairmen of Midland and National Westminster banks have recently written open letters to British newspapers stressing that they were committed to United Nations efforts to outlaw land mines.
